LESSON 36 OF 106·Operating Systems and the Command Line

Windows Security Model: Tokens, UAC and Active Directory Basics

How Windows decides what you may do: access tokens, what User Account Control changes about them, and why directory accounts multiply the blast radius of a single mistake.

Foundation14 min
Why this matters

Windows security is built around access tokens, integrity levels and objects that list who may do what. Most Windows privilege escalation is a mismatch between those and how an application actually uses them.

What you'll learn

  • How it works
  • The background
  • Real-world examples
  • What to look for

How it works

  • Every logged-in session has an access token describing the user, their groups and their privileges.
  • Access checks compare that token against the access control list on each object, so the same user has different access to different objects.
  • Integrity levels add a second dimension, separating what an ordinary process may read from what a service may write.
  • User Account Control runs most of the desktop as a filtered standard-user token and only elevates specific operations.
  • Active Directory extends the same model to identities across a network, which is why a local account problem can become a domain one.

The background

  • Windows NT replaced the older Windows with an explicit security model, including objects, tokens and descriptors.
  • User Account Control arrived because the standard user and administrator split was routinely undermined by applications requesting elevation constantly.
  • Active Directory and Group Policy turned Windows identity into the standard way large organisations manage access.
  • Later integrity levels, mandatory integrity control and virtualization-based security narrowed the paths from a compromised process to the system.

Real-world examples

  • An application configured to run with full administrator rights loses every boundary the operating system would otherwise provide.
  • A service account with domain administrator rights turns one application flaw into a domain compromise.
  • A stored credential on a machine can be extracted and replayed, which is why the operating system tries to limit where it can be used.

What to look for

  • Check whether any application is configured to run as administrator, and remove it if it can run without.
  • Check which accounts are in the local administrators group, since membership is persistent across restarts.
  • Notice stored credentials and machine account passwords, which are high-value targets.
  • Check that privileged actions require elevation rather than being silently performed.

Practice / apply

Use a suitable learning environment and follow the resource's instructions. Test other people's systems only with permission.

Key takeaways

  • Run day-to-day work as a standard user and elevate only for specific, visible operations.
  • Use separate, least-privileged service accounts rather than reusing an administrator account.
  • Restrict who can join local administrators and review that membership regularly.
  • Enable credential protection features your version supports, so stored secrets are harder to extract.
  • Treat any single point of failure account in the administrators group as a priority for review.
